chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A strategy gets blurry when a company tries to serve every customer, every channel, and every category with equal seriousness. That can sound ambitious, but it usually makes the field too wide to win on cleanly. Where to play matters because it decides where the strategy will actually live.

The Bounty case shows the move. The business got stronger when the company chose a better field instead of spreading effort across weaker ones. That is the chapter's useful lesson. Focus is not about shrinking for its own sake. It is about choosing a field where a stronger position can actually be built.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Where to play is the strategic choice that defines the field. It includes customers, channels, geographies, categories, and other boundaries that decide where the company will compete. Without that choice, the strategy stays broad and diluted because too many logics are being served at once.

Bounty works here because it shows field choice as a practical decision rather than a slogan about focus. The chapter's point is not that narrower is always better. It is that the field must be chosen deliberately enough to support a real route to win.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Breadth often flatters leaders because it lets them protect every attractive market and channel at once. It also weakens the strategy because the field never gets sharp enough for a real edge. Where to play is the correction. It forces the company to choose the ground where it intends to fight.

Bounty is the proof case. The business improved when the field got tighter and more deliberate. The chapter's edge is simple: a strategy with no chosen field is still hiding from choice.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Most teams say they want growth in a way that leaves the field blurred. They want more customers, more channels, more relevance, and more reach. That language can sound ambitious because it protects everything at once. The problem is that it rarely forces a real field choice. Until the company decides where it will actually play, the strategy keeps pretending that every customer and route deserves equal seriousness.

That is why where to play follows winning aspiration so quickly. A company that intends to win now has to decide where that intention will live. The field is not just geography. It can include customer segment, channel, category, price tier, and even parts of the value chain. Those boundaries matter because they decide what kind of advantage can make sense later. A business in the right geography can still have the wrong segment. A business with the right customers can still have the wrong channel. The field has to be chosen, not inherited blindly.

Bounty gives the chapter its strongest proof case. The business improved when the company chose a stronger playing field instead of spreading attention across weaker ones. Geography mattered. Segments mattered. The case works because it shows focus as a practical field judgment rather than a moral lecture about discipline. But the chapter also keeps one limit visible. Narrowing is not automatically strategic. The chosen field still has to support a believable route to win.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Where to play is the strategic choice that gives the company a field. Without it, the strategy stays too broad because it is trying to satisfy too many customers, channels, categories, and geographies at the same time. The chapter argues that this breadth often gets praised as ambition when it is really avoidance. A company that refuses to choose a field usually refuses the exclusions that real strategy requires.

The chapter treats field choice as multi-dimensional. Geography matters, but so do customer segments, channels, categories, price tiers, and other boundaries that define where the company will compete. This matters because where to play is upstream from how to win. If the field is blurred, the later advantage choice usually blurs with it. The company ends up with diffuse effort instead of a deliberate game.

Bounty is the chapter's main anchor because it shows a business getting stronger through field choice rather than generic effort. The chapter uses that case to warn against three common traps: trying to serve everyone, trying to buy your way into a better game, and treating the current field as fixed forever. But the chapter is not arguing that smaller is always better. A narrow field with no plausible route to win is still weak strategy. The field has to be chosen for force, not just reduced for neatness.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Breadth is one of the easiest ways to hide from strategy. A team says it wants more customers, more channels, more geographies, and more relevance, and the room treats that appetite as ambition. Usually it is the opposite. It is a refusal to choose a field hard enough to matter. Where to play is the correction because it forces the company to decide where its effort will actually count.

That choice is broader than many leaders admit. The field is not only a map. It is also the segment, the channel, the category, the price tier, and sometimes the stage of the business system you want to occupy. Blur any of those and the later strategy starts serving incompatible logics. The company calls the result flexibility. The market usually experiences it as dilution.

Bounty is the warning and the model. The business improved when the field stopped trying to cover weaker ground and started concentrating on a stronger one. The chapter then goes after the habits that keep teams from making that move: serving everyone, buying your way out, and treating the inherited field like a prison. But it also keeps the harder limit in place. Narrowing the field is not impressive by itself. If the chosen ground still offers no believable way to win, the company has only made its weakness more disciplined.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The chapter's hardest correction is that breadth often feels like ambition because it protects possibility. A team can say it wants more customers, more channels, more regions, and more relevance, and the language sounds energetic because it includes so much. But inclusion is exactly what keeps the field from getting clear. When every segment and route stays protected, the strategy never has to decide where its winning aspiration will actually live.

Where to play matters so much because it is the move that gives the strategy a field instead of a blur. The field is not only geography. It can include customer segment, channel, category, price tier, and even parts of the value chain. Those boundaries matter because later advantage depends on them. The same company can be well positioned for one segment and badly positioned for another, even inside the same country. A good channel can become a weak one if it mismatches the customer or the value logic. The chapter pushes the reader to see field choice as a strategic architecture problem, not as a map exercise.

Bounty gives the argument its strongest shape because the business improved when the field was chosen more deliberately. The lesson is not that small is automatically strong. The lesson is that the company had to identify where a winning position was structurally possible and stop treating weaker ground as equally deserving of effort. The case matters because it turns focus into judgment rather than virtue.

The traps the chapter identifies all try to protect leaders from that judgment. Serving everyone avoids exclusion. Buying your way out avoids the harder work of choosing and earning a field. Treating the current field as fixed avoids imagination. Each trap offers relief from discomfort. Each one also weakens the strategy by postponing the moment when the field gets named clearly enough to shape the rest of the cascade.

The chapter also keeps an important limit visible. Narrowing the field can still fail. A company can choose a smaller game and remain badly positioned inside it. Focus alone does not create force. The chosen field has to support a believable route to advantage later. Where to play is not a self-contained answer. It is a preparation move that has to stay accountable to how to win.

That leaves the chapter with a live tension. How narrow is strategically useful, and when does narrowing stop sharpening the game and start shrinking it into irrelevance? The next chapter matters because it will test the field choice against the harder question of advantage. Choosing the ground is necessary, but only the next step can show whether the ground can actually be won.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Where to play matters because it turns aspiration into a real field. Without that move, the strategy stays diluted by too many customers, channels, geographies, and categories being protected at once. The chapter's deeper claim is that this breadth often gets praised as ambition when it is actually avoidance. A company that refuses to choose a field usually refuses the exclusions that would make later strategic commitments possible.

The field is multi-dimensional. Geography matters, but customer segment, channel, category, price tier, and vertical scope can matter just as much. This is why where to play cannot be reduced to market size or country selection. A business can be in the right geography and still be trapped in the wrong segment. It can pursue the right customer through the wrong channel. Once those mismatches appear, the later how-to-win choice has to carry more contradiction than it can handle.

Bounty is the chapter's practical proof because the business got stronger when the field became more deliberate. The important move was not effort expansion. It was a better judgment about where a strong position was structurally possible. That is what makes the case valuable. It teaches that focus is not a character trait. It is a field-choice discipline.

The chapter then attacks the habits that weaken that discipline. Trying to serve everyone dilutes the offer. Trying to buy your way into a better game postpones strategic judgment. Treating the current field as fixed kills the imagination required to reframe the game. These are different errors, but they converge on the same weakness: the field remains underchosen.

The limit matters just as much as the correction. A narrow field is not automatically a strong field. A company can concentrate itself into a space where it still lacks a believable route to win. In that case focus has become tidier, not better. The chapter keeps this boundary alive because where to play only earns its value when it sets up a real advantage choice later.

That is the threshold it leaves open. How narrow is useful, and how do you distinguish strategic focus from disciplined irrelevance? The next chapter is needed because only a how-to-win answer can prove the field choice was strong rather than merely smaller.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Breadth is one of strategy's most expensive disguises. It sounds ambitious because it keeps more markets, segments, channels, and categories alive at once. Leaders can call that optionality, coverage, or reach. Usually it is a refusal to choose the field hard enough for the strategy to gain force. Until the ground is chosen, the company is still protecting too many excuses.

Where to play is not a minor logistics question. It is the move that gives the strategy terrain. And the terrain is more than geography. It is the segment, the channel, the category, the price point, and sometimes the layer of the business system you want to occupy. Blur those boundaries and the strategy has to serve conflicting logics at the same time. The company calls that flexibility. The market feels the dilution.

Bounty matters because the business improved when the field stopped spreading effort across weaker ground and started concentrating on a stronger one. The chapter uses that case to show that focus is not a virtue signal. It is judgment about where a business can actually build a position. The case still works under thinner source support because its function is structural, not ornamental.

The three traps all protect leaders from making that judgment. Serving everyone protects comfort. Buying your way out protects pride. Treating the inherited field as fixed protects habit. Different stories, same weakness: the company still has not chosen the ground hard enough.

But the chapter refuses shallow focus worship too. A smaller field is not automatically stronger. If the ground still offers no believable route to advantage, the company has only made its weakness more disciplined. That is the real limit. Focus without a route to win is not strategy. It is concentrated drift.

The next move matters because once the ground is chosen, the company has to prove it can build an edge there. Without that proof, the where-to-play choice is still unfinished. Choosing the field is necessary. Choosing the win condition on that field is what turns necessity into strategy.

examples.title: Talia's Team Wants Every Customer at Once

scenario.gentle: Talia opens the planning file and sees five target customer groups, three channels, and two price tiers all marked 'priority.' Browser tabs for each segment are still open across the top of her screen, and she can already feel the plan turning muddy.
scenario.direct: Talia's team claims it has a growth strategy, but the field is still spread across too many customer groups, channels, and pricing logics to create force.
scenario.competitive: Talia is staring at a classic avoidance pattern: every field looks protected because nobody wants the pain of choosing one hard enough.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask which customer group and route give the company the best chance to build a strong position first. Demote the rest from equal priority until the field is real.
whatToDo.direct: Collapse the field to the customer, channel, and price logic that can plausibly support a winning position. Treat the other options as deferred, not simultaneous.
whatToDo.competitive: Make the plan cut ground. If every segment survives as a top priority, the strategy still has no chosen field.

whyItMatters.gentle: The broader the field stays, the harder it becomes to make later strategic choices feel clear.
whyItMatters.direct: Without a chosen field, later advantage decisions have to serve too many incompatible logics at once.
whyItMatters.competitive: Blur at the field level guarantees softness later.

examples.title: Marcus Learns Why the Judges Called It Too Broad

scenario.gentle: Marcus's case competition team pitched a solution for students, local businesses, alumni, and campus administrators all in one recommendation. The judges wrote 'too broad' twice in the margin, and Marcus now has to explain why.
scenario.direct: Marcus's team tried to serve too many audiences at once, so the recommendation never established a real field.
scenario.competitive: Marcus got the brutal but accurate verdict: broad enough to mention everyone, weak enough to win with nobody.

whatToDo.gentle: Rebuild the recommendation around one audience whose needs and route to impact can be served clearly first.
whatToDo.direct: Choose the single field that gives the solution a coherent customer and channel logic, then let the rest fall behind it.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop trying to impress every audience. Pick the one field the team can actually own in the room.

whyItMatters.gentle: A solution that tries to reassure everyone rarely feels sharp to anyone.
whyItMatters.direct: Where-to-play weakness usually shows up as a recommendation that cannot prioritize its own logic.
whyItMatters.competitive: If the field is vague, the pitch becomes a compromise machine.

examples.title: Imani Names the Field Instead of the Dream

scenario.gentle: Imani says she wants to start a newsletter 'for people interested in culture and ideas.' Her friend stares at the notebook on the kitchen table and asks who that actually means.
scenario.direct: Imani has named an aspiration but not a field. The audience is too broad to guide the voice, channel, or offer.
scenario.competitive: Imani has a dream audience and no chosen field.

whatToDo.gentle: Turn the audience into a more exact field by naming who the newsletter is for, where those readers already pay attention, and what kind of problem or curiosity it will serve.
whatToDo.direct: Define the field across audience, channel, and category instead of hiding inside a broad interest label.
whatToDo.competitive: Choose the ground precisely enough that the newsletter stops trying to charm everyone at once.

whyItMatters.gentle: The surprising part is that a narrower audience can make the work feel more alive, not less ambitious.
whyItMatters.direct: Field choice creates voice and relevance by removing unnecessary breadth.
whyItMatters.competitive: Specificity often increases force faster than reach increases prestige.

scenario.gentle: Rafael reviews a product plan that targets premium customers through a bargain-heavy retail route. The spreadsheet rows line up cleanly, but the logic does not.
scenario.direct: Rafael's team chose a customer field and a channel field that pull against each other.
scenario.competitive: Rafael found the hidden fracture: the strategy wants one field and routes through another.

whatToDo.gentle: Check whether the channel reinforces the customer and price logic or quietly undermines it. If it undermines it, change the field choice before chasing execution details.
whatToDo.direct: Audit the field dimensions together. Do not treat customer, channel, and price tier as separate choices if they are creating contradiction.
whatToDo.competitive: Fix the field before you optimize the mismatch.

whyItMatters.gentle: A field can look chosen on paper and still be fighting itself underneath.
whyItMatters.direct: Where-to-play decisions fail when their boundaries are individually reasonable but collectively unstable.
whyItMatters.competitive: Misfit inside the field is still field failure.

examples.title: Noa Stops Treating the Old Audience Map as Fate

scenario.gentle: Noa inherits leadership of a student entrepreneurship club that has targeted the same audience for four years simply because 'that is who we always pitch to.' The club keeps getting polite attendance and weak traction.
scenario.direct: Noa's team is stuck in the immutable-field trap. It is treating the inherited audience map as a fact instead of a choice.
scenario.competitive: Noa inherited a field and almost inherited the excuse not to rethink it.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask whether the current audience is still the strongest field for the club's goals, or only the most familiar one. Then test a more deliberate field choice.
whatToDo.direct: Challenge the inherited playing field directly. Reframe the audience question before assuming the club must stay in the same game.
whatToDo.competitive: Break the habit that says legacy equals logic.

whyItMatters.gentle: The common trap is thinking the field was given by history when it is really being preserved by habit.
whyItMatters.direct: Treating the current field as fixed kills imagination before strategy even starts.
whyItMatters.competitive: Inherited maps feel safe because they spare leaders the pain of redesign.

examples.title: Felix Narrows the Goal Without Shrinking the Win

scenario.gentle: Felix wants to build a freelance design practice and has been pitching every kind of client he can imagine. After months of scattered outreach, he tries narrowing to a smaller field that still pays well and fits his strongest work.
scenario.direct: Felix's first field was broad enough to feel ambitious and weak enough to produce little traction. The reset is not about becoming smaller for its own sake. It is about choosing ground that can still support a win.
scenario.competitive: Felix stops calling scattershot outreach ambition and starts choosing a field he can actually take.

whatToDo.gentle: Choose the client field that fits both your strongest work and a believable path to demand, then let the rest wait.
whatToDo.direct: Narrow the field only where the narrowing increases the odds of building a real position.
whatToDo.competitive: Cut to the ground where the edge can actually show up. Ignore the rest until that ground works.

whyItMatters.gentle: The perspective shift is that focus is useful when it preserves a stronger route to success, not when it merely shrinks the ambition.
whyItMatters.direct: This is the chapter's limit in action: narrower is only better if it still supports a believable route to win.
whyItMatters.competitive: Smaller became smarter only because the field still had force inside it.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Where to play matters because it gives the strategy a real field. Breadth can feel ambitious, but the strategy only gains force when the ground is chosen deliberately.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: The where-to-play choice defines the field across customers, channels, categories, geography, and related boundaries. Without that choice, the rest of the strategy stays diluted.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: Stop mistaking broad appetite for strategic range. The strategy gets real when the ground gets chosen hard enough to matter.

questions.prompt: What does where to play mean in this chapter?
choices: Choosing the field where the company will compete
Writing a market-size forecast
Picking only a geography and nothing else

explanation.gentle: The chapter treats where to play as the field-defining choice, not as a forecasting exercise.
explanation.direct: Where to play means choosing the boundaries of competition, including more than geography alone.
explanation.competitive: The right answer gives the strategy ground. The other two only gesture at analysis.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter use Bounty?
choices: To show that smaller brands should always leave global markets
To show that stronger field choice can improve a business
To prove that channel choice never matters

explanation.gentle: Bounty matters because the case shows focus as a strategic field judgment.
explanation.direct: The example demonstrates that better playing-field choices can strengthen the business more than generalized effort can.
explanation.competitive: Bounty is evidence that smarter ground beats wider blur.

questions.prompt: A team says every customer segment and channel is still a top priority. What is the clearest diagnosis?
choices: The team is wisely preserving all options
The field has not been chosen hard enough yet
The strategy is finished because the list is comprehensive

explanation.gentle: Protecting every field at once usually means the choice has not become real yet.
explanation.direct: This is breadth as avoidance. Without a chosen field, later strategic force remains weak.
explanation.competitive: Equal protection across every field is the tell that nobody accepted the cut.

questions.prompt: Talia's product plan targets premium customers through a bargain-heavy retail route. What should she notice first?
choices: The customer and channel field choices are fighting each other
The premium customer is always wrong
Only the execution timeline needs to change

explanation.gentle: The plan's problem is the mismatch between field boundaries, not just the schedule.
explanation.direct: Where-to-play choices can fail when individually reasonable boundaries create a collectively unstable field.
explanation.competitive: The field is fractured before the execution work even starts.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter insist that where to play is more than geography?
choices: Because segment, channel, category, and related boundaries also shape the field
Because geography never matters in strategy
Because field choice should be delayed until the very end

explanation.gentle: The field can be wrong in several ways even when the geography is right.
explanation.direct: The chapter broadens the idea of field choice beyond geography because many strategic mismatches happen in segment, channel, and category logic.
explanation.competitive: A map alone cannot save a blurred field.

questions.prompt: Noa inherited the same audience map her club has used for years and assumes it must stay that way. Which trap is she in?
choices: The immutable-field trap
The premium-pricing trap
The capability-overload trap

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns against treating the current field as fate instead of choice.
explanation.direct: This is the immutable-field trap: inherited boundaries are being preserved without fresh strategic judgment.
explanation.competitive: Habit is pretending to be logic here.

questions.prompt: Imani says her newsletter is for 'people interested in culture and ideas.' What is the chapter's main critique?
choices: The audience is broad enough that the field still is not chosen clearly
She should always choose geography first
The idea is too creative for strategy work

explanation.gentle: The aspiration may be real, but the field is still too loose to guide voice or route.
explanation.direct: A broad audience label does not define the customer, channel, or category boundaries clearly enough.
explanation.competitive: She named a dream, not the ground.

questions.prompt: What do the chapter's three main traps have in common?
choices: They all reduce the need for later capabilities
They all postpone the pain of making a real field choice
They all require the company to shrink immediately

explanation.gentle: Serving everyone, buying your way out, and treating the field as fixed all help leaders delay the harder choice.
explanation.direct: The common denominator is avoidance: each trap protects the organization from choosing the ground clearly.
explanation.competitive: Different stories, same dodge. The field stays underchosen.

questions.prompt: Why is a smaller field not automatically a stronger strategy?
choices: Because narrower focus can still point the company toward a field with no believable route to win
Because strategy always improves with maximum coverage
Because field size never affects advantage

explanation.gentle: The chapter's limit is clear: focus only helps if the chosen field can still support a win.
explanation.direct: A smaller field is still weak if the business cannot build an advantage on that ground.

questions.prompt: Once the field is chosen clearly, what does the strategy need next?
choices: A reason the company can beat the alternatives on that field
A return to broad market appetite
A delay on all further strategic choices

explanation.gentle: Choosing the field sets up the next question rather than finishing the strategy.
explanation.direct: The next move is how to win: the strategy now has to define the advantage that works on the chosen ground.
explanation.competitive: Ground without edge is unfinished strategy.
